result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised reinforcement learning for discovering diverse, reusable skills without external rewards, observing that mutual-information (MI)-based methods yield policies that are distinguishable but fail to sufficiently explore state space. The key insight is to directly maximize distances between state distributions induced by different policies using the Wasserstein distance, rather than indirectly encouraging diversity via latent-conditioning and MI. Methodologically, WURL trains multiple policies by optimizing pairwise Wasserstein distances between their state visitation distributions, addressing challenges of scaling to N>2 policies and of amortizing per-step rewards, and demonstrates empirically better coverage and discriminability than MI baselines, with learned skills improving exploration and enabling hierarchical downstream learning.

The paper tackles referring video object segmentation (RVOS), where existing frame-wise approaches struggle to capture inter-frame relationships and temporal language cues, leading to weak video-level visual-linguistic alignment. Its key insight is that aggregating frame-level object embeddings into video-level object clusters tied to language tokens enables unified temporal modeling and stronger cross-modal alignment, improving handling of temporal expressions and segmentation stability. The proposed Semantic-assisted Object Cluster (SOC) creates groups of frame-level object embeddings associated with textual tokens to learn a joint multimodal space across time, and employs multi-modal contrastive supervision at the video level to explicitly align visual and linguistic representations. Extensive experiments on standard RVOS benchmarks show SOC substantially outperforms prior methods, demonstrating better temporal coherence and robustness to expressions describing object dynamics.

The paper addresses the problem that safety-aligned large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and that existing safeguard approaches—especially using the model to self-classify harmful prompts—suffer from poor detection due to a domain shift between the model’s trained self-censoring behavior and the classification task. The key insight is that asking the model to repeat its own outputs preserves the model’s natural alignment behavior and avoids the domain shift introduced by explicit classification, improving discrimination between safe and malicious responses without requiring fine-tuning or white-box access. The authors propose PARDEN, a lightweight safeguard that simply prompts the model to regenerate or repeat candidate outputs and then applies detection on the repeated text; empirical results on Llama-2 and Claude-2 show PARDEN substantially reduces false positives at high true-positive rates (e.g., an ~11× FPR reduction for Llama2-7B at 90% TPR) compared to baseline jailbreak detectors.

The paper tackles the challenge of end-to-end weakly supervised semantic segmentation (WSSS) from image-level labels, where existing methods produce low-quality pseudo-labels due to incomplete semantic cues. The key insight is that a network can distill richer, complementary semantic information from its own feature correspondences—using self-derived pixel/region affinities as a supervision signal—to refine its predictions without external labels. The proposed Self Correspondence Distillation (SCD) framework trains the model to match its outputs to correspondence-based targets and is combined with a Variation-aware Refine Module that enforces local consistency by computing pixel-level variation, all implemented efficiently in a Transformer-based TSCD architecture. Experiments on PASCAL VOC 2012 and MS COCO 2014 show that this self-distillation plus variation-aware refinement yields substantially better pseudo-labels and segmentation performance than prior end-to-end WSSS methods.

The paper tackles unsupervised domain adaptation for video action recognition, where models trained on a labeled source domain must generalize to an unlabeled target domain with different appearance or temporal characteristics. The key insight is that temporal contrastive learning—maximizing similarity between different-speed augmentations of the same video and minimizing similarity across videos—can align cross-domain video representations without adversarial training, and that augmenting contrastive positives via background mixing leverages shared action semantics to strengthen invariance. The method, called Contrast and Mix (CoMix), combines temporal contrastive loss on speed-augmented clips, a novel background-mixed extension that creates extra positive pairs by mixing background content while preserving action cues, and a supervised contrastive objective using target pseudo-labels to improve class discriminability; experiments show this approach outperforms prior video domain adaptation techniques.

The paper tackles understanding and designing transformer networks by asking what representation learning should achieve: compressing token distributions into mixtures of low-dimensional Gaussians on incoherent subspaces. The key insight is a unified objective called sparse rate reduction—combining lossy coding rate reduction (compression) and sparsification—that explains why transformer blocks (attention + MLP) naturally arise as alternating optimization steps on complementary parts of this objective. Methodologically, the authors derive transformer-like blocks from principled alternating updates where multi-head self-attention performs a gradient-descent-like compression step and the MLP enforces sparsity, instantiate a family of fully interpretable "white-box" architectures, and empirically show these models compress and sparsify representations on large vision datasets while achieving performance close to engineered transformers.

The paper tackles finding stationary points of nonconvex stochastic compositional optimization problems where the objective is a composition of functions and accessing exact values and Jacobians is costly or stochastic. Its key insight is that stochastic Gauss-Newton updates, when paired with appropriate stochastic estimators (classical unbiased samples or variance-reduced SARAH estimators) for both function values and Jacobians, can achieve the same O(ε^{-2}) iteration complexity as first-order methods while controlling the total stochastic oracle calls. The authors propose two algorithms—one for the expectation setting and one for the finite-sum setting—that use minibatch or SARAH-style estimators to approximate inner function outputs and Jacobians and perform Gauss-Newton steps with proven global complexity guarantees. They further provide oracle-call bounds (in expectation and with high probability) and validate the theory on synthetic and real datasets.

The paper tackles the challenge of compressing large Transformer-based language models for resource-constrained deployment without costly fine-tuning or large accuracy loss. The key insight is that a Transformer block can be redefined as modular matrix-pair components whose outputs can be reconstructed via structured, module-level low-rank approximations, enabling effective compression without gradient-based recovery. The method, called MoDeGPT, applies a theoretical framework combining Nyström approximation, CR decomposition, and SVD to each module to reduce hidden dimensions and reconstruct outputs, producing compressed models matching or exceeding prior structured compression approaches that require backpropagation. Experiments show MoDeGPT preserves 90–95% zero-shot performance at 25–30% compression, cuts compute by 98% on a 13B model, can run compression on a single GPU in hours, and improves inference throughput up to 46%.

The paper tackles catastrophic interference in continual learning, where sequential tasks share a common parameter space and thus overwrite each other. Its key insight is to assign each task a distinct low-rank vector subspace and enforce orthogonality between these subspaces (and their task gradients) so that learning one task minimally disturbs others. Concretely, the authors train networks via isometric mappings constrained on the Stiefel manifold to produce task-specific low-rank orthogonal representations and gradients, and demonstrate that this subspace orthogonalization outperforms standard experience-replay baselines (with and without memory) on standard continual classification benchmarks.

The paper addresses improving video object detection by exploiting temporal information more effectively and efficiently to boost both accuracy and speed. Its key insight is that propagating object-level representations (object queries) across frames, rather than dense pixel- or box-level features, can reduce redundant computation on non-key frames and enrich key-frame features with temporal context. The proposed QueryProp framework implements two propagation modes—from sparse key frames to dense non-key frames to avoid reprocessing every frame, and from previous key frames to the current key frame to enhance feature representation—plus an adaptive propagation gate that flexibly selects key frames; experiments on ImageNet VID show competitive accuracy with a favorable accuracy/speed trade-off.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that weakly supervised semantic segmentation models trained from image-level class labels tend to localize only small discriminative object parts rather than entire objects. The key insight is that output activations like sigmoid/softmax create an information bottleneck at the network’s final layer, selectively passing only the most discriminative information and discarding other task-relevant cues needed for full-object localization. To mitigate this, the authors remove the last activation function to reduce the bottleneck and propose a novel pooling scheme that encourages signals from non-discriminative regions to contribute to classification, thereby improving the richness of localization maps. Experiments on PASCAL VOC 2012 and MS COCO 2014 show that these simple modifications substantially enhance localization quality and set a new state-of-the-art for weakly supervised semantic segmentation.

result.text: The paper tackles the gap between the massive scaling success of language Transformers and comparatively small Vision Transformers (ViTs), aiming to demonstrate whether ViTs can be reliably trained at LLM-like scales and what benefits arise. Its key insight is that with a carefully designed training recipe—addressing stability, efficiency, and optimization nuances—dense ViTs can be scaled to tens of billions of parameters and yield systematic gains in downstream performance and desirable emergent properties. Methodologically, the authors develop and validate a set of engineering and training practices (e.g., stability fixes, optimization and regularization choices, data and compute strategies) to train a 22B-parameter ViT, then evaluate it across frozen feature linear-probe and downstream tasks to show improved accuracy with scale, better robustness, enhanced alignment with human shape/texture perception, and improved fairness–performance tradeoffs.

result.text: The paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in continual learning by proposing a nonparametric approach that uses per-task kernel classifiers trained from a small episodic memory, avoiding interference between tasks. The key insight is that kernel methods—implemented via kernel ridge regression on stored coresets and enhanced by learning task-specific kernels—can prevent task interference without replaying data through a shared parametric model. Methodologically, the authors store a small subset of examples per task, fit kernel ridge regressors using either fixed kernels or learned data-driven kernels via variational random Fourier features (treating the random basis as latent and inferring a variational posterior from each coreset), which yields more informative, compact per-task kernels and reduces memory while maintaining strong continual learning performance.

result.text: The paper tackles the slow convergence and limited spatial precision of DETR’s global Transformer attention for end-to-end object detection. The key insight is that attention need not be dense over the entire image feature map—attending to a small, learned set of spatial sampling points around a reference is sufficient and more efficient. They introduce Deformable DETR, which replaces full attention with deformable attention modules that predict reference points and a sparse set of offsets and weights per query, aggregating features only at those sampled locations across multi-scale feature maps; this yields faster training (≈10× fewer epochs) and improved detection, particularly for small objects, on COCO.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of current video-text pre-training methods that extract frame-level features and thus ignore the spatio-temporal object structure that aligns naturally with nouns in text. Its key insight is that learning region-level representations—by clustering patch features and aggregating them into semantic regions with learnable masks, then modeling their spatio-temporal relations—yields more meaningful visual units for aligning with language than raw pixels or detector-based proposals. The proposed RegionLearner module quantizes patch features via clustering, generates learnable masks to merge fragmentary patches into coherent regions, and models dependencies across regions over time to produce region-aware video representations; it requires no object supervision and is computationally efficient, and is pre-trained on WebVid2M and CC3M and shown to improve video-text retrieval.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between image-level self-supervised representations and the need for dense, pixel-level features for tasks like segmentation and detection. Empirically, VADeR transfers effectively to multiple dense prediction tasks and outperforms both ImageNet supervised pretraining and strong unsupervised baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised video domain adaptation for action recognition, where domain shifts arise from both spatial (appearance) and temporal (motion) differences between source and target videos. Its key insight is that spatial and temporal divergences can be more effectively handled by disentangling video generation into separate static (appearance) and dynamic (motion) latent factors, so that domain-specific static content can be isolated and temporal differences addressed independently. The authors propose Transfer Sequential VAE (TranSVAE), a generative framework that models cross-domain video synthesis from static and dynamic latents and incorporates novel constraints on these latents plus adversarial learning at frame and video levels to remove spatial domain information and align temporal dynamics. Experiments on UCF-HMDB, Jester, and Epic-Kitchens show that TranSVAE reduces domain gaps and outperforms several state-of-the-art unsupervised adaptation methods.

result.text: The paper tackles whether convolution and attention are necessary for high-performance vision models by asking if a purely MLP-based architecture can compete on image classification. The key insight is that separate, repeated MLPs can be used to mix features along the channel dimension and across spatial patches—i.e., one MLP operates per patch to mix channel information and another operates across patches to mix spatial information—so that complex spatial and cross-channel interactions can emerge without convolution or attention. result.text: The paper addresses stochastic multi-level compositional optimization where the objective is a composition of several smooth (possibly nonconvex) functions and existing solvers either have suboptimal sample complexity or require large batch sizes. The key insight is that a tailored multi-level variance-reduction scheme can control stochastic error across composition levels to attain information-theoretically optimal sample complexity without large per-iteration batches, and that stage-wise scheduling or PL/convex structure can further accelerate convergence. Concretely, the authors propose SMVR (and a stage-wise variant) which achieves O(1/ε^3) samples to find an ε-stationary point in the general nonconvex case, O(1/ε^2) for convex objectives, and O(1/(μ ε)) for μ-PL (hence μ-strongly convex) problems, and they introduce an adaptive-learning-rate version (Adaptive SMVR) that retains these optimal rates while improving empirical speed. All complexities match known lower bounds in ε and μ and are obtained without using prohibitively large batch sizes.

result.text: The paper tackles efficient compression of Transformer models for resource-constrained deployment, noting that prior weight-focused low-rank approximations perform poorly for transformers and require large labeled datasets to fine-tune. Its key insight is that activations (features) in transformer layers are empirically low-rank even though the learned weight matrices are not, so compressing outputs rather than weights yields more faithful reduction. Building on this, the authors introduce AAFM, which adaptively determines per-layer compression structure and locally compresses each linear layer's output features in a few-shot, unsupervised manner, followed by a global fine-tuning stage GFM that holistically optimizes the compressed network; both stages use only a small unlabeled sample set. The method achieves substantial parameter and latency reductions with minimal accuracy loss (e.g., 33% parameters removed and 18.8% throughput gain with only 0.23% ImageNet accuracy drop using 2K unlabeled images), transfers to NLP tasks, and generalizes well to downstream tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses how to learn shared representations for multi-task reinforcement learning that capture both commonalities and task-specific differences while avoiding redundant or collapsed features. Its key insight is that enforcing orthogonality among expert-generated representations encourages diversity and a compact shared subspace that can be flexibly combined to represent different tasks. The proposed method, Mixture Of Orthogonal Experts (MOORE), builds a mixture-of-experts encoder whose expert outputs are orthogonalized via a Gram–Schmidt process to form a shared subspace, and a task-conditioned gating mechanism selects relevant combinations from that subspace to produce task-specific representations for policy learning. Evaluated on MiniGrid and MetaWorld, MOORE outperforms prior baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on MetaWorld.

The key insight is that sequential, recurrent training of skills—rather than simultaneous optimization—combined with an intrinsic reward that explicitly encourages state coverage can avoid overlap-induced blocking and foster more diverse behaviors. result.text: The paper tackles Natural Language Video Localization (NLVL), the task of finding the temporal segment in a long untrimmed video that corresponds to a natural language query, noting that existing one-stage methods—anchor-based and anchor-free—either rely on heuristic, fixed candidates or fail to capture segment-level interactions. The key insight is to combine the strengths of both paradigms in a two-stage framework that uses an anchor-free mechanism to produce high-quality boundary proposals and then applies a segment-level multimodal matching stage to fully exploit visual–language interactions. Concretely, the proposed Boundary Proposal Network (BPNet) first generates candidate segments with precise boundaries via an anchor-free model, then passes each candidate through a visual–language fusion layer and a matching score rating layer to produce alignment scores. Experiments and ablation studies on Charades-STA, TACoS and ActivityNet-Captions show BPNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

The paper addresses the lack of standardized, reproducible evaluation for jailbreak attacks that coax large language models into producing harmful or policy-violating outputs, noting inconsistent metrics and inaccessible artifacts in prior work. Its key insight is that a shared, open, and evolving benchmark—combining a curated repository of adversarial prompts, a representative behavior dataset, and a unified evaluation protocol—can make jailbreak research comparable, transparent, and reproducible while enabling systematic tracking of defenses. The authors present JailbreakBench, which packs (1) an evolving collection of jailbreak artifacts, (2) a 100-behavior dataset aligned with OpenAI policies drawn from prior literature and new cases, (3) a standardized threat model, chat templates, system prompts, and scoring functions implemented in an open evaluation framework, and (4) a public leaderboard to record attack and defense performance across models.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised video representation learning, aiming to capture both motion and appearance features from unlabeled video for downstream tasks like action recognition, a challenge because prior self-supervised tasks either yield imprecise speed labels or overemphasize motion at the expense of appearance. The key insight is that relative playback speed between two clips provides more consistent, stable supervision for motion perception than absolute speed labels, and that pairing this with an appearance-focused task that forces the model to detect appearance differences prevents collapse to motion-only features. The method, RSPNet, jointly trains two heads: a relative-speed classification head that predicts which of two clips is faster (thus learning motion cues) and an appearance-difference head that predicts whether clips come from the same scene/appearance, and this combined objective produces strong unsupervised features that improve action recognition and retrieval—achieving 93.7% on UCF101 without labeled pre-training.

result.text: The paper tackles catastrophic forgetting in continual learning by enabling positive forward transfer from related past tasks while avoiding interference with them. The key insight is to identify a layer-wise "trust region" of previously learned tasks that are most relevant to a new task using the norm of the gradient projection onto subspaces spanned by task inputs, and then selectively reuse their frozen weights via a learned layer-wise scaling. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of temporal action segmentation in long, untrimmed videos under limited frame-wise labels by introducing the first semi-supervised approach for this task. The key insight is that effective semi-supervised segmentation requires unsupervised frame-level representations that respect temporal proximity, multi-resolution structure, and variable action lengths and orderings across videos, which can then be merged iteratively with supervised learning. The authors propose Iterative Contrast-Classify (ICC): a pipeline that learns TCN-based frame representations via clustering that incorporates time-proximity and multi-resolution similarity, and alternates between contrastive-style representation refinement and classification using available labels. ICC progressively improves as more labeled videos are added and achieves near fully-supervised performance with only 40% labeled data, while also boosting frame-wise accuracy on standard benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the high memory and computation cost of training and running Vision Transformers (ViTs) by exploring how to integrate sparsity throughout the entire training-to-inference lifecycle rather than pruning after training. Its key insight is that dynamically training and maintaining a fixed small parameter budget—jointly optimizing weights and connectivity while also optionally sparsifying attention heads and input tokens—can yield large efficiency gains without hurting, and sometimes even improving, accuracy. Methodologically, the authors propose end-to-end sparse (co-)training that repeatedly prunes-and-grows unstructured or structured (head-level) connections during training and introduce a learnable token selector to co-sparsify input patches; the result is a single sparse subnetwork trained from scratch that reduces FLOPs and runtime yet preserves or improves ImageNet performance across multiple ViT backbones.

result.text: The paper tackles task-free continual learning, where models must avoid catastrophic forgetting without task boundaries, by improving the usefulness of stored replay examples whose relevance degrades as the model updates. Its key insight is that slightly editing stored examples in input space via gradient-based updates can make them more "challenging" for the model—i.e., increase their future loss—while keeping them similar to the original exemplars, thereby yielding stronger rehearsal signals during replay. The proposed method, Gradient-based Memory EDiting (GMED), computes gradients that maximize upcoming loss with respect to stored examples and applies constrained input-space updates to those examples online; GMED is modular and can be applied on top of existing memory-based continual learning algorithms. Empirical results show GMED consistently improves performance and achieves state-of-the-art on five of six benchmark datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of noisy pseudo-mask labels in weakly-supervised semantic segmentation (WSSS), where high-confidence but incorrect pixels degrade model training. Its key insight is that noisy pixels often exhibit unstable confidence when the prediction response range is perturbed, so estimating uncertainty by scaling model responses can reveal which supervision signals are unreliable. The proposed method, URN, repeatedly scales the prediction map to simulate response variations, computes per-pixel uncertainty from the resulting prediction variability, and uses these uncertainties as weights in the segmentation loss to down-weight noisy supervision; this simple uncertainty-aware reweighting yields substantial improvements and sets new state-of-the-art results on PASCAL VOC 2012 and MS COCO 2014.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of near out-of-distribution (OOD) detection—distinguishing inputs that are semantically close but not from the training distribution—by asking how far large-scale pre-trained transformers can push performance across modalities. The key insight is that scale and unsupervised or multi-modal pre-training endow transformer representations with much stronger separation between in- and near-outlier data, and these representations are especially amenable to scarce outlier supervision (few-shot outlier exposure) or even class-name-only cues. result.text: The paper addresses the high per-update computational cost of variance-reduced stochastic optimization methods (e.g., SVRG, SpiderBoost), which use large and small batch gradients and thus require roughly double the operations of SGD. The key insight is that large-batch gradients can be exploited to estimate and leverage inherent gradient sparsity, so that applying a randomized top-k sparsification reduces computation while preserving variance-reduction benefits. The method introduces a random-top-k operator that combines top-k selection with randomized coordinate sampling to sparsify gradients, integrates this into a SpiderBoost-style variance-reduced algorithm, and proves matching or better worst-case guarantees while empirically showing improved speed and accuracy across image classification, NLP, and sparse matrix factorization tasks, supported by gradient-entropy measurements that quantify sparsity.

result.text: The paper addresses optimization of nonconvex functions that do not satisfy standard smoothness assumptions, a gap that makes many gradient-based methods suboptimal for common ML objectives (e.g., high-order polynomials, exponentials). Its key insight is that a new notion—α-symmetric generalized-smoothness—unifies and extends previous generalized-smooth conditions and still admits descent properties strong enough to support optimal complexity guarantees. Methodologically, the authors prove fundamental properties and descent lemmas for this function class and then design a deterministic normalized gradient descent that attains the optimal iteration complexity O(ε^{-2}), while showing that the SPIDER variance-reduction method achieves the optimal stochastic sample complexity O(ε^{-3}), thereby demonstrating that generalized-smooth nonconvex optimization can be solved as efficiently as the standard smooth case.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of compressing large Transformer-based language models to reduce memory and compute without sacrificing performance. The key insight is that a weight matrix can be more effectively approximated as the sum of a low-rank component that captures coherent, expressive neuron behavior and a sparse component that removes incoherent, non-expressive elements, with each component compensating for limitations of the other. The proposed LoSparse method jointly learns a low-rank factorization and a structured pruning mask for each weight matrix, balancing rank reduction and sparsity so pruning increases the diversity of low-rank representations while low-rank factors preserve expressive capacity lost to pruning. Empirical evaluation on NLU, QA, and generation benchmarks shows LoSparse outperforms existing compression techniques, delivering better trade-offs between model size and task performance.

result.text: The paper tackles extreme compression of large language models—reducing model size to extremely low bit rates (2–3 bits per parameter) so they can run on end-user devices without large accuracy loss. The key insight is to adapt and extend multi-codebook Additive Quantization (AQ) for LLMs by making quantization input-adaptive and by jointly optimizing codebooks across transformer blocks, which together preserve model fidelity at very low bit widths. Their method, AQLM, learns additive, input-dependent codebook assignments for weight matrices and optimizes codebook parameters jointly across layers, producing Pareto-optimal accuracy-vs-size tradeoffs below 3 bits and substantially improving 2-bit compression. They also deliver practical, highly optimized GPU/CPU implementations for token generation that match or beat FP16 speed while using far less memory.

result.text: The paper addresses how to improve stability (remembering past tasks) and plasticity (adapting to new tasks) in continual learning by quantifying how individual training examples differentially influence these two objectives when past data cannot be retained. The key insight is that influence functions (IFs) can reveal S- and P-aware example importance, but exact IFs are impractical for deep nets due to expensive Hessian-inverse computations, so simulating IF computation with lightweight meta-steps can approximate per-example influence. The authors propose MetaSP, which mimics the two core IF steps to estimate S- and P-influences, formulates a dual-objective optimization to fuse those influences into a single SP-Pareto-optimal score, and uses that fused influence to guide parameter updates and rehearsal buffer selection; experiments show substantial gains over prior CL methods on task- and class-incremental benchmarks.

args.text: We propose Sequential OT-guided Skill Discovery: at each stage, train a new skill by maximizing a Sinkhorn-regularized Wasserstein distance between its state-occupancy distribution and the mixture of occupancies from previously learned skills, using dual OT potentials computed over the replay buffer to yield dense per-step intrinsic rewards. This fuses WURL’s distributional repulsion with ReST’s sequential schedule to avoid overlap and collapse, while using environment-linearized costs (as in IBOL) to shape the transport ground metric toward long-range, diverse transitions. To softly steer the repertoire toward downstream families without external rewards, we incorporate a small set of demonstrations and add an OTR-style transport term that attracts selected skills toward demo manifolds while repelling others, jointly achieving both wide coverage and targeted behaviors.

result.text: The paper tackles referring image segmentation, aiming to produce high-quality masks for an object described by a language expression, and addresses limitations of existing iterative refinements that rely on RNNs or stacked attention layers. The key insight is to use a continuously updated query that starts from language features and is iteratively refined with object features so that, at each step, multi-modal features strongly correlated with the query are strengthened while less relevant features are suppressed, enabling a gradual shift from localization-focused to segmentation-focused representations. The method implements this semantics-aware dynamic localization and refinement by repeatedly updating the query and modulating vision-language feature maps to recover missing object parts and remove extraneous regions, and it is designed to be simple, model-agnostic, and easily plugged into prior architectures, yielding consistent improvements on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and G-Ref.

result.text: The paper tackles the gap in evaluating and attacking moderation guardrails in large language models (LLMs), noting that many jailbreak benchmarks ignore prompts that trigger input- or output-level moderation filters; this leaves both evaluation and red-teaming incomplete. The key insight is that effective jailbreaks must target both input filters (via crafted prefixes) and output filters (by encoding harmful content using non-standard “cipher characters” produced by a surrogate model that mimics the guardrail), enabling harmful content to evade detection and decoding back into readable form. The authors introduce JAMBench, a 160-instruction benchmark spanning four risk categories and multiple severity levels designed to reliably trigger guardrails, and propose JAM, a two-part attack combining jailbreak prefixes to bypass input-level defenses with a fine-tuned shadow model that generates cipher-character outputs to slip past output-level filters; experiments on four LLMs show JAM substantially increases jailbreak success and reduces filtering compared to baselines.

Its key insight is that applying contrastive learning at the regional (pixel or region) level, focusing on a sparse set of hard negative pixels, encourages features to be more discriminative across class boundaries and yields smoother, faster-converging segmentation. args.text: We propose controllability-aware Wasserstein skill discovery that measures diversity between skills via optimal transport over discounted visitation (successor) distributions in a dynamics-weighted feature space. The ground cost is a Mahalanobis metric induced by local linearization and controllability Gramians, encouraging separation along directions the agent can actually influence while de-emphasizing uncontrollable variability. Concretely, we learn successor features to approximate discounted occupancies and optimize a sliced-Wasserstein objective with projections adapted to the controllable subspace; dual critics amortize per-step intrinsic rewards, and distance-to-barycenter scaling supports many skills. This unifies distributional diversity with dynamics-aware representations and successor-feature estimation, yielding broader, more reachable coverage and improved downstream transfer.

args.text: We propose Adversarial Subspace Probing (ASP) for continual learning: maintain per-layer low-rank bases of important directions for past tasks and enforce orthogonality during new-task updates. Periodically, synthesize small "probe exemplars" by editing replay items to maximize projected gradient energy onto protected subspaces, thereby exposing interference modes that static bases miss. The probe gradients then drive rank-1 updates and rotations of the stored bases and adaptively tighten or relax orthogonality constraints where collisions are detected, yielding data-driven subspace protection without growing memory. ASP decouples discovery of interference directions from standard loss optimization and should outperform static projection/orthogonalization and vanilla memory editing in both task- and task-agnostic settings.

result.text: The paper tackles efficient and accurate video salient object detection (VSOD), noting that prior temporal models like LSTM/C3D or vanilla non-local attention either propagate motion slowly or capture motion-agnostic global context with prohibitive cost. Its key insight is that motion cues can be better captured by constraining self-attention to follow the natural continuity of object trajectories, and that organizing such constrained attentions at multiple spatial-temporal scales yields both richer motion modeling and computational savings. Concretely, the authors propose a Constrained Self-Attention (CSA) operation that restricts attention to locally coherent temporal neighborhoods to emphasize motion-consistent interactions, and stack CSA modules in a pyramidal design (PCSA) to handle objects of different sizes and speeds, producing a fast, end-to-end network that outperforms prior methods in accuracy while running at about 110 FPS.

result.text: The paper tackles the high computational and memory cost of training vision transformers (ViTs) by identifying million-scale training data redundancy as a root cause of slow training and limited generalization. The key insight is that sparsity can be introduced not only in model weights but also hierarchically in the data and attention computations—across three levels: reducing the number of training examples, pruning image patches (tokens) per example, and sparsifying token-to-token attention connections. Methodologically, the authors propose Tri-Level E-ViT, an end-to-end framework that applies a hierarchical redundancy reduction scheme to selectively sample examples, drop unimportant patches, and mask attention links during training, which yields substantial training speedups while preserving or even improving accuracy across ViT variants. Extensive experiments demonstrate concrete speedup-accuracy tradeoffs (e.g., ~15% faster with marginally better Top-1 accuracy on DeiT-T/S), validating that exploiting data-level sparsity can make ViT training more efficient.

The key insight is that the mean component removed by Pre-LN is redundant in the main residual branch, so by explicitly compressing or eliminating this zero-mean information one can reduce LN to an RMS-style normalization without loss of arithmetic functionality. The authors introduce Compressed RMSNorm (CRMSNorm) and corresponding Pre-CRMSNorm Transformers that perform a lossless compression of zero-mean vectors and prove formal equivalence between Pre-LN, Pre-RMSNorm, and Pre-CRMSNorm during training and inference, enabling direct substitution. Empirically, replacing Pre-LN with Pre-(C)RMSNorm yields identical behavior while cutting training and inference time by about 1%–10%.

result.text: We propose controllability-aware Wasserstein skill discovery that measures diversity between skills via optimal transport over discounted visitation (successor) distributions in a dynamics-weighted feature space. This unifies distributional diversity with dynamics-aware representations and successor-feature estimation, yielding broader, more reachable coverage and improved downstream transfer.

result.text: The paper tackles the scalability bottleneck of Transformers by replacing their quadratic-cost softmax attention with a linear-time, linear-space mechanism that preserves full-rank attention without assuming sparsity or low-rank structure. The key insight is that softmax attention can be accurately and unbiasedly estimated via a novel random-feature technique—FAVOR+ (Fast Attention Via positive Orthogonal Random features)—which yields positive, orthogonal random features that enable low-variance, provably convergent approximations of the attention kernel. args.text: We propose OccluFlow-QueryProp, a video object detector that propagates object queries along occlusion-aware motion tubes rather than frame-synchronous grids. Each query predicts a short-horizon motion trajectory via lightweight flow-conditioned dynamics and attends with deformable sampling only to sparse spatio-temporal points on this tube, while a depth-ordered occlusion module gates aggregation to maintain object permanence through overlaps. An adaptive key-frame scheduler selects updates based on per-query motion entropy, reducing redundant computation under slow motion and reinforcing features during fast motion or occlusion. This design preserves QueryProp’s efficiency while boosting robustness to high-speed motion and occlusions with minimal overhead.

The key insight is that a late interaction mechanism—computing token-wise similarities and taking a maximum over visual tokens for each textual token—can inject fine-grained supervision into a contrastive loss, yielding word–patch level alignment without changing model architectures or preventing offline precomputation. result.text: The paper tackles the inefficiency of autoregressive transformer inference caused by large key-value (KV) caches whose memory grows with sequence length and batch size. Its key insight is that a model can learn to compress KV caches online with varying compression ratios across heads and layers, preserving representational fidelity where it matters while aggressively compressing where it does not. The proposed method, Dynamic Memory Compression (DMC), retrofits pretrained LLMs via brief continued pretraining (no extra parameters) so they emit compressed KV representations during inference, enabling up to 7× throughput and up to 4× cache size reduction on Llama 2 models while maintaining downstream performance; DMC also outperforms and can be combined with prior techniques like grouped-query attention and eviction policies.

args.text: We propose TrajProp, a flow-conditioned, trajectory-constrained object-query propagation for real-time video object detection. Building on query propagation and deformable attention, each object query predicts a 2D velocity and uncertainty that generate dynamic reference points and restrict cross-frame sampling to a motion-consistent tube, concentrating aggregation where the object actually moves and reducing cost. To handle occlusions, we add a lightweight depth-order head and an amodal memory inspired by flow-conditioned object-centric layers: the model freezes visual updates when occlusion probability is high while maintaining pose via flow, resuming feature updates upon reappearance. Coupled with adaptive frame selection, this trajectory- and occlusion-aware propagation boosts accuracy on fast motion and heavy-occlusion clips at similar compute to keyframe baselines.

result.text: We propose Sequential OT-guided Skill Discovery: at each stage, train a new skill by maximizing a Sinkhorn-regularized Wasserstein distance between its state-occupancy distribution and the mixture of occupancies from previously learned skills, using dual OT potentials computed over the replay buffer to yield dense per-step intrinsic rewards. This fuses WURL’s distributional repulsion with ReST’s sequential schedule to avoid overlap and collapse, while using environment-linearized costs (as in IBOL) to shape the transport ground metric toward long-range, diverse transitions. To softly steer the repertoire toward downstream families without external rewards, we incorporate a small set of demonstrations and add an OTR-style transport term that attracts selected skills toward demo manifolds while repelling others, jointly achieving both wide coverage and targeted behaviors.

args.text: We propose Causal-Uncertain Self-Correspondence Distillation (CU-SCD) for weakly supervised semantic segmentation. Instead of trusting raw self-derived pixel affinities, we compute correspondences in both the original image and a context-intervened view that removes co-occurrence bias, and retain only links stable under intervention while weighting each pixel’s distillation target by an uncertainty score from response-scaling perturbations. A dual-view loss aligns predictions to these debiased, uncertainty-weighted correspondences and selectively propagates only high-stability links across images that share the same tags to improve object completeness without importing spurious context. args.text: We propose JKO-Skills: learn a population of skills by simulating Wasserstein gradient flows over their discounted occupancy measures. Each skill performs a proximal JKO step that trades staying close to its previous occupancy with decreasing an energy that repels it from other skills (via W2 over state visitation), attracts selected skills toward a few demonstration trajectories, and shapes the ground cost using environment linearization/controllability to favor long-range, feasible transitions. We amortize these implicit distributional updates into dense per-step intrinsic rewards using dual OT critics over successor-feature embeddings, and alternate skills’ JKO steps to avoid interference via sequential scheduling. This yields stable, coverage-seeking yet targetable repertoires that respect dynamics geometry and can be steered with a handful of demos.

result.text: The paper tackles referring video object segmentation (RVOS), where existing frame-wise approaches struggle to capture inter-frame relationships and temporal language cues, leading to weak video-level visual-linguistic alignment. Its key insight is that aggregating frame-level object embeddings into video-level object clusters tied to language tokens enables unified temporal modeling and stronger cross-modal alignment, improving handling of temporal expressions and segmentation stability. The proposed Semantic-assisted Object Cluster (SOC) creates groups of frame-level object embeddings associated with textual tokens to learn a joint multimodal space across time, and employs multi-modal contrastive supervision at the video level to explicitly align visual and linguistic representations. Extensive experiments on standard RVOS benchmarks show SOC substantially outperforms prior methods, demonstrating better temporal coherence and robustness to expressions describing object dynamics.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of detecting and removing backdoors in diffusion generative models, which can be triggered by stamped inputs (e.g., noisy seeds with a patch) to force the model to produce a target image. The key insight is that backdoors produce anomalous, learnable behavior under distribution shifts in the diffusion sampling process, so intentionally perturbing or shifting the input/noise distribution and observing model outputs reveals and isolates malicious mappings without harming normal generation. The authors implement Elijah, a framework that applies targeted distribution shifts and statistical tests to detect backdoored models and then neutralizes the backdoor by retraining or fine-tuning under shifted distributions to erase the trigger-conditioned mapping, demonstrating near-perfect detection and near-zero retained backdoor effect across hundreds of DDPM, NCSN, and LDM models with multiple samplers and attack types while preserving generation quality.

args.text: I propose Continual Mixture of Orthogonal Subspaces (CMOS) for task-agnostic continual learning: build a fixed-capacity mixture-of-experts encoder whose expert outputs are orthogonalized on the Stiefel manifold, while maintaining for each expert a compact activation-subspace dictionary updated online via GPM-style SVD sketches. For a new data stream, compute per-layer gradient projections onto stored subspaces to estimate relatedness and use a trust-region gate to freeze and rescale related experts while routing genuinely novel signal to a reserve expert trained strictly in directions orthogonal to all claimed subspaces. This combines non-interference from subspace projection with positive forward transfer via selective expert reuse, without task IDs or network growth, and works replay-free but can incorporate a small buffer if available. We hypothesize improved stability–plasticity trade-offs and sample efficiency on class- and task-incremental benchmarks.

The authors introduce XLVINs, which learn a latent state representation and a graph-structured transition model, then execute value-iteration-like computation entirely in that latent space using neural graph-algorithmic modules trained with contrastive self-supervision so the latent planner aligns with true value iteration; this yields substantial data-efficiency gains across control, navigation, and Atari tasks.

args.text: We propose Language-Conditioned Spatio-Temporal Track Tokenization (LST3), which forms adaptive track-level tokens by jointly clustering frame patches into unsupervised regions and linking them across time with motion cues, while allowing the token budget to vary with scene complexity. args.text: Unify token pruning, attention sparsification, and expert routing in Vision Transformers by optimizing a compute-aware sparse rate reduction Lagrangian that treats representation learning as coding tokens with a mixture of low-dimensional, incoherent subspaces under an explicit per-operation compute budget. Attention provides soft assignments (posterior responsibilities) to subspaces, while MLPs and routing gates perform proximal sparsification; tokens whose marginal rate reduction falls below a learned threshold are dropped or merged, and head/expert activations are penalized proportional to their compute. Alternating E/M-like updates with learnable dual variables adapt per-example budgets so that tri-level sparsity (examples, tokens, and attention links/experts) emerges automatically with token-level interpretability. This principled objective should stabilize end-to-end sparse co-training and achieve MoE-level capacity–accuracy at lower FLOPs than ad-hoc pruning by aligning routing decisions with rate–distortion theory.

result.text: We propose TrajProp, a flow-conditioned, trajectory-constrained object-query propagation for real-time video object detection. Building on query propagation and deformable attention, each object query predicts a 2D velocity and uncertainty that generate dynamic reference points and restrict cross-frame sampling to a motion-consistent tube, concentrating aggregation where the object actually moves and reducing cost. result.text: The paper addresses the problem that safety-aligned large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and that existing safeguard approaches—especially using the model to self-classify harmful prompts—suffer from poor detection due to a domain shift between the model’s trained self-censoring behavior and the classification task. The key insight is that asking the model to repeat its own outputs preserves the model’s natural alignment behavior and avoids the domain shift introduced by explicit classification, improving discrimination between safe and malicious responses without requiring fine-tuning or white-box access. The authors propose PARDEN, a lightweight safeguard that simply prompts the model to regenerate or repeat candidate outputs and then applies detection on the repeated text; empirical results on Llama-2 and Claude-2 show PARDEN substantially reduces false positives at high true-positive rates (e.g., an ~11× FPR reduction for Llama2-7B at 90% TPR) compared to baseline jailbreak detectors.

The paper addresses the problem that weakly supervised semantic segmentation models trained from image-level class labels tend to localize only small discriminative object parts rather than entire objects. The key insight is that output activations like sigmoid/softmax create an information bottleneck at the network’s final layer, selectively passing only the most discriminative information and discarding other task-relevant cues needed for full-object localization. To mitigate this, the authors remove the last activation function to reduce the bottleneck and propose a novel pooling scheme that encourages signals from non-discriminative regions to contribute to classification, thereby improving the richness of localization maps. Experiments on PASCAL VOC 2012 and MS COCO 2014 show that these simple modifications substantially enhance localization quality and set a new state-of-the-art for weakly supervised semantic segmentation.

result.text: The paper addresses the inefficiency of caching key-value pairs in decoder-only Transformers for long-context and large-model inference, which incurs large GPU memory and prefill latency costs. The key insight is that a two-stage "decoder-decoder" design—consisting of a self-decoder that builds a single global KV cache and a cross-decoder that reuses that cache via cross-attention—can replicate decoder-only behavior while caching KV pairs only once. YOCO implements this by stacking a cross-decoder on top of a self-decoder so that the heavy global context is encoded once and then attended to cheaply, enabling early-exit prefilling without changing final outputs. Empirically, this architecture preserves model quality while dramatically reducing inference memory, improving prefill latency and throughput across model sizes and context lengths (demonstrated up to 1M tokens with high retrieval accuracy).

The paper addresses how to learn shared representations for multi-task reinforcement learning that capture both commonalities and task-specific differences while avoiding redundant or collapsed features. Its key insight is that enforcing orthogonality among expert-generated representations encourages diversity and a compact shared subspace that can be flexibly combined to represent different tasks. The proposed method, Mixture Of Orthogonal Experts (MOORE), builds a mixture-of-experts encoder whose expert outputs are orthogonalized via a Gram–Schmidt process to form a shared subspace, and a task-conditioned gating mechanism selects relevant combinations from that subspace to produce task-specific representations for policy learning. Evaluated on MiniGrid and MetaWorld, MOORE outperforms prior baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on MetaWorld.

result.text: The paper tackles Natural Language Video Localization (NLVL), the task of finding the temporal segment in a long untrimmed video that corresponds to a natural language query, noting that existing one-stage methods—anchor-based and anchor-free—either rely on heuristic, fixed candidates or fail to capture segment-level interactions. The key insight is to combine the strengths of both paradigms in a two-stage framework that uses an anchor-free mechanism to produce high-quality boundary proposals and then applies a segment-level multimodal matching stage to fully exploit visual–language interactions. Concretely, the proposed Boundary Proposal Network (BPNet) first generates candidate segments with precise boundaries via an anchor-free model, then passes each candidate through a visual–language fusion layer and a matching score rating layer to produce alignment scores. Experiments and ablation studies on Charades-STA, TACoS and ActivityNet-Captions show BPNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

result.text: We propose TrajProp, a flow-conditioned, trajectory-constrained object-query propagation for real-time video object detection. Building on query propagation and deformable attention, each object query predicts a 2D velocity and uncertainty that generate dynamic reference points and restrict cross-frame sampling to a motion-consistent tube, concentrating aggregation where the object actually moves and reducing cost. To handle occlusions, we add a lightweight depth-order head and an amodal memory inspired by flow-conditioned object-centric layers: the model freezes visual updates when occlusion probability is high while maintaining pose via flow, resuming feature updates upon reappearance. Coupled with adaptive frame selection, this trajectory- and occlusion-aware propagation boosts accuracy on fast motion and heavy-occlusion clips at similar compute to keyframe baselines.

args.text: We propose a query-conditioned spatio-temporal tokenizer that produces a variable number of tube tokens by clustering patch trajectories into coherent, motion-aware segments guided by the language expression. Unlike image-only semantic tokenizers, the tubes maintain temporal continuity and are formed via cross-modal clustering that weights features by query-relevant nouns, attributes, and verbs, then feeds these tokens to a lightweight context-modulated matcher for RVOS/NLVL. Training leverages counterfactual video–text augmentations to create hard negatives that differ in a single temporal or attribute cue, enforcing attribute-specific and temporal grounding at the tube level with a contrastive objective. This plug-in front end enhances temporal coherence and disambiguation among similar instances, improving downstream segmentation/localization stability and fine-grained grounding.

args.text: We propose EgoExo-SlotUDA, a parameter-efficient unsupervised domain adaptation framework for egocentric–exocentric action recognition that aligns object-centric dynamic latents across views and datasets. We first obtain object slots using a temporal feature-similarity signal from a frozen image backbone augmented with lightweight spatial and temporal adapters, then disentangle each slot into static (appearance) and dynamic (motion) factors and perform cross-domain contrast at the slot-dynamic level with multi-rate positives for speed invariance, background-mixed positives for appearance robustness, and time-reversal hard negatives. A simple curriculum with pseudo-label refinement and dynamic-time-warp matching further handles temporal misalignment across views while preserving fine-grained hand–object interactions. This unifies object-centric video modeling, parameter-efficient adaptation, temporal contrastive UDA, and view-invariant ego–exo alignment to improve transfer without full finetuning.

We propose Spectral-Routed Hybrid Attention (SRHA), a ViT block that routes tokens to specialized experts based on a lightweight, differentiable spectral score. All complexities match known lower bounds in ε and μ and are obtained without using prohibitively large batch sizes.

result.text: The paper tackles the growing memory burden of key-value (KV) caches during decoding in autoregressive transformer LLMs, which becomes prohibitive at long sequence lengths and large batch sizes. Its key insight is that, beyond sharing key/value heads across query heads as in Multi-Query Attention (MQA) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), adjacent transformer layers can also share key and value heads without materially harming accuracy. The authors propose Cross-Layer Attention (CLA), an attention block design that reuses KV heads across neighboring layers to halve the KV cache size relative to MQA, and they validate this by training 1B- and 3B-parameter models showing CLA achieves a Pareto improvement in the memory-versus-accuracy tradeoff. This enables inference with longer contexts and larger batches while maintaining near-MQA performance.

The paper tackles continual learning—training limited-capacity models on a stream of unknown, sequential tasks without catastrophic forgetting—by addressing the speed, online applicability, and hyperparameter sensitivity limitations of prior meta-learning approaches. The key insight is that modulating per-parameter learning rates via a look-ahead meta-update (connecting to hypergradients and meta-descent) provides a flexible, efficient mechanism to reduce interference between old and new tasks while remaining compatible with an episodic memory buffer. result.text: The paper tackles actor-and-action video segmentation with language queries, where models must localize and segment the object described by a natural-language phrase across frames—a task made difficult by similar-looking objects and the need for fine-grained spatiotemporal reasoning. The key insight is that dynamic convolutions used to fuse language and vision should incorporate spatial context and temporal motion, because generating kernels solely from local region features and text ignores surrounding cues that disambiguate similar instances. result.text: The paper addresses weakly supervised segmentation, where training uses partial annotations (image tags, boxes, points, scribbles) that either lack precise pixel localization or broad coverage, making standard label propagation and refinement methods siloed and suboptimal. The key insight is to reframe the problem as semi-supervised metric learning so that pixels belonging to the same semantic segment are mapped to similar features while different semantics are pushed apart, enabling a unified treatment of diverse weak annotations. The authors propose four pixel-to-segment contrastive relationships—capturing low-level similarity, semantic annotation, co-occurrence, and feature affinity—that serve as priors to drive feature learning from any combination of partial labels; unlabeled pixels contribute by participating in intra-image grouping and inter-image discriminative learning. Implemented as a universal weakly supervised segmenter trained with these contrastive cues, the method improves segmentation performance on benchmarks like Pascal VOC and DensePose.

args.text: We propose Slot-Disentangled Contrastive Adaptation (SDCA) for unsupervised video domain adaptation under severe appearance/viewpoint shifts (e.g., ego↔exo). SDCA first extracts object-centric tubes via motion-biased slot discovery that emphasize hands and active objects, then encodes each tube with a disentangled model that separates static appearance from dynamic motion while explicitly purging domain cues from the static latent. Cross-domain alignment is applied to the dynamic latent using temporally aware contrastive objectives—speed-augmentation positives and reversed-time hard negatives—and class prototypes refined with target pseudo-labels; the object-centric focus reduces spurious background dependence and obviates the need for background mixing. We hypothesize SDCA yields stronger cross-domain action recognition and fine-grained cross-view retrieval by aligning motion semantics while isolating domain-specific appearance.

I propose a subspace-aware, tri-level dynamic ViT that couples activation low-rank compression with token and expert sparsity to adapt compute per image and per token. result.text: The paper tackles catastrophic forgetting in continual learning by enabling positive forward transfer from related past tasks while avoiding interference with them. The key insight is to identify a layer-wise "trust region" of previously learned tasks that are most relevant to a new task using the norm of the gradient projection onto subspaces spanned by task inputs, and then selectively reuse their frozen weights via a learned layer-wise scaling. result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of speeding up exact dynamic programming for reducible combinatorial optimization problems by replacing costly value or policy computations with learned approximations. Its key insight is that for problems decomposable into sequential decision steps, deep neural networks can be trained to emulate stepwise value or policy functions, enabling much faster approximate DP while preserving solution structure. The authors propose two variants—value-based NDP, where DNNs estimate the value of each choice at a step, and policy-based NDP, where DNNs predict the best decision—and train networks progressively from small to larger problem sizes, then fine-tune them jointly. They validate NDP on assignment, TSP, and talent scheduling tasks, showing substantial runtime reductions with modest optimality loss.

result.text: The paper tackles task-agnostic continual learning, where a model must sequentially learn new tasks without access to task identities at inference and therefore must both retain old-task performance (stability) and learn new classes (plasticity). The key insight is that replay-based approaches conflate two distinct objectives when training on mixed old and new data—(a) distinguishing new classes from old classes and (b) distinguishing among new classes—and that decoupling these losses enables different weighting to better balance stability and plasticity. The proposed method, Loss Decoupling (LODE), splits the new-task loss into separate components for those two objectives and applies distinct weights during replay-based updates, allowing targeted optimization for class separation versus preservation of old knowledge. Empirical results show that LODE yields better trade-offs and outperforms state-of-the-art replay-based continual learning methods across multiple datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of noisy pseudo-mask labels in weakly-supervised semantic segmentation (WSSS), where high-confidence but incorrect pixels degrade model training. Its key insight is that noisy pixels often exhibit unstable confidence when the prediction response range is perturbed, so estimating uncertainty by scaling model responses can reveal which supervision signals are unreliable. The proposed method, URN, repeatedly scales the prediction map to simulate response variations, computes per-pixel uncertainty from the resulting prediction variability, and uses these uncertainties as weights in the segmentation loss to down-weight noisy supervision; this simple uncertainty-aware reweighting yields substantial improvements and sets new state-of-the-art results on PASCAL VOC 2012 and MS COCO 2014.

result.text: The paper tackles parameter-efficient transfer learning from large image-pretrained models to video action recognition, addressing the lack of temporal knowledge in image models and the high cost of full fine-tuning. The key insight is that a compact, learnable spatio-temporal module can be injected into a frozen image backbone to endow it with temporal reasoning while only updating a small fraction of parameters per task. They propose the ST-Adapter, a lightweight adapter with built-in spatio-temporal reasoning blocks inserted into the network that add temporal interactions across frames and spatial processing within frames, enabling effective image-to-video adaptation at roughly an 8% per-task parameter overhead (about 20× fewer updated parameters than prior methods). Extensive experiments show ST-Adapter matches or exceeds full fine-tuning and state-of-the-art video models on action recognition while remaining far more parameter-efficient.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap in current multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs), which struggle to unify image comprehension and generation within a single autoregressive Transformer and thus lack open-world emergent abilities. The key insight is that images must be tokenized into a 1D sequence of semantically rich, causally ordered tokens that mirror the left-to-right autoregressive structure of text and are optimized to balance discriminativeness and reconstructability. The authors propose SEED, an image tokenizer that produces position-independent, high-level visual tokens trained for both reconstruction and semantic separation, and integrate these tokens into LLaMA to train SEED-LLaMA via standard next-token prediction and instruction tuning on interleaved text–image data. The resulting model performs scalable multimodal autoregression and demonstrates strong unified comprehension and generative capabilities, including emergent multi-turn in-context multimodal generation.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of creating effective token-level jailbreak attacks that coax large language models into generating harmful content despite discrete token optimization being difficult. The key insight is to relax the discrete token selection into a continuous optimization that is gradually sparsified, yielding vectors that smoothly transition from dense continuous representations to sparse, near-discrete token triggers and thereby bridging the gap between continuous and discrete search. The method, Adaptive Dense-to-Sparse Constrained Optimization (ADC), performs constrained continuous optimization with an adaptive schedule that increases sparsity over iterations to produce compact token triggers, and experiments on Harmbench show ADC outperforms previous token-level jailbreak techniques across multiple open-source LLMs in both effectiveness and efficiency.

The paper tackles weakly supervised semantic segmentation, aiming to generate accurate pixel-level masks from only image-level labels by leveraging relationships across images. Its key insight is that grouping images and explicitly modeling their semantic dependencies yields more reliable pseudo ground-truths than treating images independently, because inter-image interactions help reveal complete object responses and suppress spurious common cues. Methodologically, the authors build a graph neural network where images are nodes connected via an efficient co-attention mechanism to capture pairwise relations, introduce a graph dropout layer to avoid overfocusing on shared semantics, and perform end-to-end iterative message passing to refine pseudo labels for training segmentation models, achieving state-of-the-art results on PASCAL VOC 2012 and COCO.

args.text: We propose Slot-Adapter UDA, a parameter-efficient framework that injects two lightweight adapters into a frozen image backbone—one static and one dynamic—that operate on object-centric slot tokens for unsupervised video domain adaptation. Slots are obtained via temporal feature-similarity grouping (and optionally hands–object crops); the static adapter learns domain-invariant appearance using background-mixed positives and slot-level supervised/pseudo-label contrast, while the dynamic adapter adds temporal interactions trained with speed perturbations and reversed-time negatives to align motion across domains. We further introduce a slot-transport consistency loss that swaps static slots from source with dynamic slots from target (and vice versa), emulating disentangled transfer without a full generative model. This combines the strengths of contrastive temporal augmentation, object-centric grouping, and disentangled alignment while updating only a small fraction of parameters through adapters.

result.text: The paper tackles the high computational cost of Vision Transformers (ViTs) at inference and training time by reducing the number of tokens processed without retraining or with minimal training. The key insight is that many tokens are redundant (e.g., multiple tokens representing parts of the same object or across frames) and can be merged into representative tokens with little accuracy loss, so selectively combining similar tokens yields large speedups. The proposed method, Token Merging (ToMe), uses a lightweight, general matching algorithm to pair and merge similar token embeddings during forward passes (optionally applied during training), thereby cutting token count and compute while preserving information; empirically ToMe doubles throughput for large ViTs on images, videos, and audio with only ~0.2–0.4% accuracy/mAP drops and can also accelerate MAE fine-tuning.

result.text: The paper tackles event-based object detection, aiming to overcome suboptimal hand-crafted 2D conversions of asynchronous, sparse event-camera data that limit detection under high-speed motion and poor illumination. Its key insight is that a learnable 3D event representation combined with dual memory aggregation—capturing both long-term context and short-term spatial-temporal correlations—better preserves and leverages information in event streams for detection. Methodologically, the authors convert positive and negative polarity events into x-y-t grids forming pillar tensors, then feed these into a Dual Memory Aggregation Network (DMANet) where long memory is stored in adaptive convLSTM hidden states and short memory is obtained by computing spatial-temporal correlations between neighboring-time pillars, producing detections. Experiments on an event-based automotive dataset show the learned representation and dual-memory aggregation substantially improve event-based object detection.

The paper tackles speeding up reinforcement learning by automatically deriving potential functions for potential-based reward shaping, a task as hard as learning value functions itself. The key insight is to treat the environment as a graph and use Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) to perform message passing from rewarding states so that rewards can be propagated through state-space structure to produce informative potentials. Concretely, the method constructs a graph over states (or learned state embeddings), trains a GCN to diffuse signals originating at rewarding states under a probabilistic-inference perspective of RL, and uses the resulting propagated values as potential functions to reshape rewards and accelerate downstream policy learning. Empirical results show substantial improvements in both tabular and high-dimensional control tasks.

The key insight is that effective jailbreaks must target both input filters (via crafted prefixes) and output filters (by encoding harmful content using non-standard “cipher characters” produced by a surrogate model that mimics the guardrail), enabling harmful content to evade detection and decoding back into readable form. Slots are obtained via temporal feature-similarity grouping (and optionally hands–object crops); the static adapter learns domain-invariant appearance using background-mixed positives and slot-level supervised/pseudo-label contrast, while the dynamic adapter adds temporal interactions trained with speed perturbations and reversed-time negatives to align motion across domains. We further introduce a slot-transport consistency loss that swaps static slots from source with dynamic slots from target (and vice versa), emulating disentangled transfer without a full generative model. This combines the strengths of contrastive temporal augmentation, object-centric grouping, and disentangled alignment while updating only a small fraction of parameters through adapters.

args.text: We propose Canonicalize-Repeat-Detect (CRD), a guardrail wrapper that first self-canonicalizes model outputs—constrained paraphrasing that transliterates confusables, normalizes leetspeak, and deciphers likely simple ciphers—then applies PARDEN-style repeat-based detection on the canonicalized text. The canonicalizer is a small LM (or constrained decoding routine) trained to invert common obfuscations, including cipher-character emissions used to evade output filters, and to abstain when semantic confidence is low, with a backoff to multi-pass paraphrase-by-consensus across models. result.text: The paper tackles the limitation of Class Activation Maps (CAMs) in image-level weakly supervised semantic segmentation, where CAMs focus on discriminative regions and lack segmentation-specific completeness. args.text: We propose Token–Expert Co-Sparse ViT, which jointly optimizes token sparsity and expert sparsity under a global FLOPs budget to attain large capacity with low per-image compute. args.text: We propose Lifted-XLVIN: a latent value-iteration planner that operates directly on lifted, predicate- and object-centric graphs to achieve strong combinatorial generalization across object counts and task instances. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of bias in local inverse-Hessian (second-order) estimates used in distributed optimization: when each machine computes a sketched or subsampled estimate from a small batch, averaging these biased local estimates slows convergence relative to the true full-data solution. The key insight is that by using surrogate sketches drawn from determinantal point processes—whose bias for inverse-Hessian estimation can be computed exactly—and by appropriately shrinking the regularization used on each machine, the bias can be eliminated analytically. Concretely, the method modifies standard sketching to produce surrogate sketches and prescribes scaling the local regularizer from λ to λ′ = λ·(1 − d_λ/m), where d_λ is the λ-effective dimension and m the sketch size, thereby producing unbiased local estimates whose averaged second-order direction yields provably and empirically faster distributed convergence.

args.text: We propose TAViT: a temporally adaptive semantic tokenizer for videos that produces a variable-length sequence of entity-centric tokens with persistent identities, allocating more tokens to regions with rich motion or interactions and fewer to static background. It extends region-level unsupervised grouping to the spatiotemporal domain with learnable masks and cross-frame association, and learns language-aligned tokens via late-interaction token-level contrast and video-level object-cluster supervision. The resulting discrete video tokens plug natively into autoregressive multimodal LLMs trained under unified next-token prediction, with a video-trained teacher distilling temporal commonsense into the LLM. This design targets stronger RVOS, natural-language video localization, and open-vocabulary grounding, while enabling controllable video generation by prompting over token streams tied to tracked entities.

We propose Canonicalizer-Guard, a universal cipher-resilient moderation layer that meta-learns to invert unseen text encodings and obfuscations before and after the main guardrail. Trained via self-supervised mixtures of synthetic ciphers, homoglyph/spacing/noise transforms, and multilingual paraphrases, it produces a small set of canonical candidates (decoded, transliterated, translated, paraphrased) and applies consensus moderation augmented with repeat-based self-checks to minimize domain-shift errors. Deployed both on inputs and outputs, Canonicalizer-Guard aims to neutralize cipher-character output evasion and non-natural-language prompt jailbreaks, and can be co-optimized with robust system-suffix defenses. We expect substantial gains on JAMBench and JailbreakBench, particularly against CipherChat-style ciphers and adaptive token-level attacks.

args.text: We propose Query-Temporal Semantic Tokenization (QTST) for video-language tasks: a query-conditioned tokenizer that adaptively groups spatiotemporal patches into variable-length entity and event tokens aligned with the nouns and verbs in the text. result.text: The paper addresses why preference-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to "jailbreaking"—adversarial prompts that elicit harmful or undesired behavior—despite fine-tuning efforts like RLHF.
